venue_now: not shown in the text: the file is arXiv 2404.13076v1 (15 Apr 2024) with no venue header; the search note gives NeurIPS 2024 (oral) from OpenReview and Semantic Scholar, which this reviewer could not check from the text
what_it_is: A study of whether LLM evaluators recognise their own outputs and whether that self-recognition drives self-preference. On news summarisation (1,000 articles each from XSUM and CNN/DailyMail), Llama-2-7b-chat, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 judge pairs or single summaries written by themselves, the other two models or humans, both for quality (self-preference) and for authorship (self-recognition). Out of the box all three show self-preference and better-than-chance self-recognition (GPT-4 73.5% pairwise). Fine-tuning GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 to raise or lower self-recognition, plus control fine-tunes on unrelated tasks, yields a linear relation between self-recognition and self-preference, which the authors present as evidence towards, not proof of, a causal link.
domain: news summarisation (XSUM, CNN/DailyMail); no technical or reasoning content
size: 2 datasets x 1,000 articles (500 for fine-tuning, 500 for evaluation); 3 evaluator/generator models (Llama-2-7b-chat, GPT-3.5, GPT-4) plus human summaries; fine-tuned variants of GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 (self-recognition with 2, 10, 500 examples and 5 control tasks per dataset)
source_of_items: existing summarisation datasets (human reference summaries) plus summaries generated by the three models at temperature zero
evaluation: LLM judge in pairwise (which summary is better / which is yours, both orders averaged) and individual (1-5 Likert rating / yes-no authorship) formats, scored from token probabilities; correlation of self-recognition and self-preference scores across fine-tuned models and per example (Kendall's tau)
human_validation: none: no human quality ratings are collected; the authors note that showing disproportionate self-preference would require ground-truth quality annotation and offer only indirect evidence (paired self-preference scores summing to more than 1) (pp. 7-8)

engtrace_use.explanation: Candidate, not cited in the May paper. It is the standard citation for the mechanism behind the reviewers' circularity objection: the May Tribunal's GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3 scored traces from a 27-model roster that included GPT-5 itself and other GPT, Claude and Gemini models, so judges were scoring their own and their families' outputs. This paper shows LLM evaluators favour their own generations and that the strength of the preference tracks how well they recognise their own text (pp. 1-6). EngTrace's residual judge (MiMo-V2.5-Pro) generates no trace on the roster, which removes the self-evaluation channel this paper measures; the paper says nothing direct about cross-family similarity (its discussion only conjectures that a rating 'can be inflated simply because it's most similar to the model used for evaluation', p. 7), so for MiMo's documented exposure to Claude the relevant evidence is the family and similarity papers (Spiliopoulou 2025, Goel 2025, Li 2026), not this one. Its setting is subjective summary quality, not correctness, so it does not show self-preference on binary milestone verdicts.

suggested_wording: LLM evaluators favour their own generations, and the strength of this self-preference rises with their ability to recognise their own text (Panickssery et al., 2024); a judge that also sits on the evaluated roster, as in the May Tribunal, is therefore not a neutral evaluator.
facts_to_cite: LLM evaluators (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2) disproportionately favour summaries written by themselves over those by other LLMs and humans on XSUM and CNN/DailyMail (p. 2, Figure 4 p. 4).
Out of the box, all three models exceed 50% accuracy at telling their own summaries from others'; GPT-4 is 73.5% accurate against two other LLMs and humans (p. 2).
Fine-tuning on 500 examples raises self-recognition above 90% for GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 (p. 2).

Across fine-tuned models, self-preference strength is linearly correlated with self-recognition, and models fine-tuned on unrelated control tasks (length, vowel count, readability, constant and random answers) fall on the same trend (Figure 1 p. 1; pp. 5-6).
The authors present this as evidence towards, not validation of, a causal link: 'our experiments can only provide evidence towards the causal hypothesis without fully validating it' (p. 7).
Pairwise judges reverse their preference when the two options are swapped at rates of 25% (GPT-4), 58% (GPT-3.5) and 89% (Llama 2) (p. 4).
Telling GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 the (swapped) source labels reverses their preference on XSUM toward the summary labelled as their own (p. 6).
No human quality labels were collected; evidence that the preference is disproportionate is indirect (pp. 7-8).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: concern with an LLM judge scoring outputs related to it, the problem EngTrace addresses by taking its residual judge from outside the roster. Lacks: generated instances, gold traces, step-level evaluation, engineering or any technical domain (summarisation only), correctness labels, human or expert validation of the judge, and any test of family (as opposed to self) preference.
notes: Paragraph: process supervision and judge validity. Must-cite as the canonical self-preference reference; pair it with a correctness-based or rubric-based self-preference result (Pombal 2026 or Spiliopoulou 2025) because this one is about subjective summary quality with three 2023-era models. The batch table's phrase 'by their fine-tuning tests causally' overstates the paper, which claims only evidence towards causality (p. 7) and calls its results 'initial evidence' (p. 8). The abstract defines self-preference against human judgements of equal quality, but the study collects none (pp. 7-8). The text file is the v1 preprint; if the revision cites the NeurIPS 2024 version, the consolidator should confirm the cited numbers there, since the camera-ready may differ. Confidence is high on the content and the recommendation, low on the venue, which rests on the search note alone.
